blocks.html:
To a big part of the world, it probably looks like something very French. But riots have always held a strange beauty.


Riots don’t have to be violent, and most of them aren’t. This piece looks at the violent side on purpose: it’s the side that feels closest, and visually the most striking.


A riot sits on a balance between complete mayhem and a kind of mechanism that moves forward. It brings together people who have the same thing in mind, who want to go somewhere, toward a place or an ideology. And art has never stopped coming back to it.


In 2008, Justice released the video for Stress. It isn’t about a riot, but it borrows the visual codes of one. What stands out is the duality. A riot is often violent, because it rises against something that doesn’t want to move, or isn’t moving enough for the people it’s supposed to serve. That’s the paradox, and the beauty of it: it’s violent for peace.

Four years later came No Church in the Wild, which went even further. Both videos were directed by Romain Gavras, and riots run through his whole body of work. From Stress to M.I.A.’s Born Free, from music videos to feature films, the visual codes of the riot keep coming back. Even as his projects grew bigger, they never left the centre.


 In 2022 he made Athena for Netflix, a full film built around a housing estate set on fire after the death of a teenager, pushing France to the edge. Even when the rest of the world wants to show a riot, it often looks through a French eye.


France has a long history of riots, resistance and revolution. Many countries do. But there is something more here, something hard to put into words. Everyone jokes about it, “the French just want to riot”, but when it starts, it’s taken seriously. It’s normal. It’s part of the society.

The consequence is that the people at the top are never really comfortable. They know they can be kicked out quickly, because it’s a right, and power is there for the people, not for the two or three guys on top.

blocks.html:
Violence is also a message. On 17 October 2026, hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets across France, and once again the same demand came back from the top: say it, but say it nicely.


The rapper Casey has named this better than anyone. Speaking about the myth of the aggressive Black person, she explains that it has always existed to disqualify people from thinking. If you’re angry, you can’t reason. In the West, anger is treated as the enemy of thought. For her, that’s paternalism: a way of saying you’re primitive, that you can’t organise your ideas, a way of disqualifying what you say. And a way of staying comfortable.


“I know you’re suffering, I’m willing to hear you, but tell me nicely, so it isn’t uncomfortable.”

Her answer: “No. Sometimes it’s a spit in your face, one I want to throw so that you understand.” What the person in power asks of the oppressed, from the comfort of their impunity, is to describe their suffering gently, with all the softness, love and tenderness required. “Isn’t that an incredible degree of insolence?”

That’s what a riot says.

Long before all of this, there was La Haine. Mathieu Kassovitz’s 1995 film showed what riots look like for the part of society that really needs them.


Thanks for reading,
